source: Honestly, my neighbours. Mrs. Baek would leave kimchi on our doorstep without a word, and other families did the same. Nobody said anything about it. That is how we got through, people just quietly helped. I try to do the same now when I see someone struggling.

source: Yes. In nineteen eighty-one I opened a little alteration shop with the sewing machine, in the front room of our new house. Within a year I had four women working for me. We did wedding dresses mostly, and school uniforms, and in the busy season we worked until midnight. By nineteen eighty-eight I had moved the shop to a real storefront on the main street.

source: That all three of my children went to university. I could not, so I made sure they did. Soyeon became a teacher, Hyunwoo an engineer, and Mina a doctor. When Mina graduated, I sat in the third row and I cried so hard that the woman next to me gave me her handkerchief. I still have that handkerchief too.

source: Minho retired in nineteen ninety-nine and then he took up gardening, which nobody expected. He grew tomatoes and peppers on the roof, in big plastic tubs, and he talked to them every morning. He passed away in two thousand and eight, in the autumn. I still water the tomatoes, although they are never as good as his.

source: Slowly. The children came every weekend for the first year, in turns, and Mina stayed with me for a month. I did not sleep in our bed for a long time, I slept on the sofa. Then one day I just did, and it was fine. Grief is strange like that, it does not go, it just changes shape.

source: I volunteer at the community centre twice a week, teaching the young girls how to sew a button and hem a skirt. They think it is old-fashioned, but they listen. And I write down my recipes for my grandchildren, because I do not want them to be lost. I have written down about forty already.

source: My mother's fish stew. She made it with whatever was left at the end of the market day, so it was never the same twice, but it always had radish and a lot of pepper. I make it every year on her birthday, which was the ninth of November, and the whole family comes.

source: Oh, did I say forty-six? I think it was actually nineteen forty-seven, I always mix it up, the papers say forty-seven but my mother always said forty-six. So, one of those.

source: To be less afraid. I was afraid of so many things, of not having enough, of what people thought. Most of the things I was afraid of never happened, and the ones that did happen, I survived. So, be kinder to yourself, and eat more, and call your mother more often while she is still there.

source: Thank you for listening. Nobody asks me these things anymore.

source: I was born in Busan, in a little house near the harbour, I think it was nineteen forty-six, in the spring. My mother always said the fishing boats were coming in the morning I was born, so there was a lot of noise and the midwife could hardly hear herself think.
title: Born in Busan near the harbour
body: I was born in Busan, in a little house near the harbour, I think it was nineteen forty-six, in the spring. My mother always said the fishing boats were coming in the morning I was born, so there was a lot of noise and the midwife could hardly hear herself think.

source: My father repaired boats. He had big hands, really big, and he did not talk much at all. He would come home smelling of tar and sawdust, and he would sit by the door and take his boots off, and that was it, that was the whole conversation for the evening. But on Sundays he took me to the pier and we watched the ships. I loved those Sundays.

source: My mother sold fish at the market. She left before dawn and came home after sunset every single day, and her hands smelled of salt. She was the one who held the family together. She could count money faster than anyone I ever met, and she never learned to read, but nobody ever cheated her, not once. Yes, she was something.

source: We lived in a shack made of scrap boards, and the wind came through the walls in winter. We had one stove for the whole family, so we all slept close to it. There were six of us in two rooms. I remember my brother Jaesung kept a little bird in a box under his bed, and he fed it rice, and it lived for almost two years.

source: I only finished fifth grade. We could not afford more. But my teacher, Mrs. Han, said I had the most beautiful handwriting in the whole school, and she gave me a pencil box as a prize when I left. I still have that pencil box, it is in the cabinet in my bedroom. It has a picture of a crane on the lid.

source: At eighteen I started at a textile factory, and I gave my whole pay to my mother. Every month, the whole envelope. She would put a little aside for me in a tin, and when I got married she gave me the tin, and there was enough in it for a sewing machine. That machine is what I started my own business with, many years later.

source: I met Minho in nineteen sixty-six, at a church supper. He was so nervous that he spilled gravy all over his shirt, and I laughed, and he went red, and that was that. We married in June of nineteen sixty-seven, in a small ceremony, because we did not have money for anything bigger.
title: I met Minho in nineteen sixty-six
body: I met Minho in nineteen sixty-six, at a church supper. He was so nervous that he spilled gravy all over his shirt, and I laughed, and he went red, and that was that. We married in June of nineteen sixty-seven, in a small ceremony, because we did not have money for anything bigger.

source: We moved to Daegu, because Minho had found work at a printing house there. The pay was better than the harbour. We rented two rooms above a tailor's shop, and the tailor, Mr. Baek, became like an uncle to us. He taught me to cut cloth, and that is how I started sewing for other people.

source: We had three children. Our first, Soyeon, was born in nineteen sixty-nine, then Hyunwoo in nineteen seventy-two, and the youngest, Mina, came along in nineteen seventy-six. I was thirty by the time Mina was born, and I was so tired, but she was the easiest of the three, she slept through the night from the second month.

source: Money, always money. There was a winter when Minho's printing house closed for three months and we ate rice with salt and nothing else. I sold my sewing machine that winter, it broke my heart, and I bought it back the next spring from the same man for twice the price. I never told Minho what I paid.

source: My people came from a little town in Poland, I think it was called Zamosc, but I never saw it myself. My father left in nineteen twenty-nine, he was nineteen, and he did not speak a word of English when he got off the boat in New York.

source: He washed dishes in a restaurant on the Lower East Side for about two years. He did not make much, maybe six dollars a week, and he slept on the floor of a cousin's apartment with four other men.

source: At a dance at the synagogue hall in nineteen thirty-four. She was a seamstress. She was not supposed to be there, her own mother did not approve of dancing, but she went anyway and he asked her to dance and she said no twice.

source: I was drafted in nineteen forty-three, I was twenty. I never talked about it much. I was in the infantry, and we crossed into France in the summer of forty-four. I don't remember all the names of the towns anymore, honestly. I lost two friends in one week, Eddie Marks and a boy from Ohio whose name I never learned.

source: My mother was waiting at the station, and she did not recognise me at first, I had lost thirty pounds. We did not say anything, she just held my face. My father was not there, he was working a double shift, he came home at midnight and sat on my bed until I woke up.

source: Yes, on the G.I. Bill. I studied engineering at City College, and I graduated in nineteen fifty. I was the first one in my family to finish college, and my mother kept the diploma in the drawer with her good tablecloth.

source: I married Ruth in nineteen fifty-two. We had two girls, Naomi and Dina. Naomi was born in fifty-four, I believe, and Dina three years later. We bought a house in Queens for eleven thousand dollars, which seemed like all the money in the world.

source: I worked for the city, designing bridges and roads, for thirty-one years. I was proud of that. I drove across the bridge I helped build every Sunday, just to look at it, and Ruth would say, Walter, it's the same bridge.

source: I never went to see my father's village. He asked me to, once, before he died, and I said maybe next year, and there was no next year. That is the thing. I think about it more than the war.
